Giffen: Chapter four. When demand slopes up: Giffen behaviour.

First, the history of a rumour. Marshall gave Giffen as his source in 1895, but no reference and no numbers. In 1947 George Stigler went looking for the claim in Giffen's writings and couldn't find it; and the evidence on bread and wheat in Britain didn't show demand sloping up. The example in most textbooks became the potato in the Irish famine of the eighteen-forties. In 1999 Sherwin Rosen argued that it couldn't be right: the price of potatoes rose because blight destroyed the crop, so the Irish could not have eaten more potatoes, whatever they wanted. That's the deeper problem. In a whole market, price and quantity move together for many reasons; Part four's identification problem again. To see a demand curve slope up, you need households, and a price that someone changes on purpose.

Theory first, with the household from Play it. Hold its twenty-one dollars fixed and let the price of coconuts run from very cheap to very dear. When coconuts are cheap, the household eats enough with money to spare, chooses by taste, and its demand slopes down like anyone's. Past about 95 cents, the calorie line starts to bind, and the household is pinned where money and calories run out together. From there, every rise in the price of coconuts means fewer fish and more coconuts: demand slopes up. Past 2 dollars 10 the household has no fish left to give up; it spends everything on coconuts, and a higher price can only mean fewer. In the middle zone the elasticity has a simple form. It depends only on how many calories a dollar buys in each food: the fewer the fish give relative to coconuts, the stronger the effect. At a dollar twenty it's nought point four three. Jensen and Miller's own figures make the same point: in Hunan a yuan bought fourteen hundred calories of rice and three hundred and thirty of pork.

That's the theory Jensen and Miller took to Hunan and Gansu. They surveyed every household three times: in April, before anyone knew about vouchers; in September, after three months with them; and in December, after they had ended. For each household, two changes in its rice consumption, matched with two changes in its price, and compared only with other households in the same town at the same time. The coefficient is the price elasticity, and it is positive if demand slopes up. And the theory told them where to look: among households poor enough to depend on rice, but not so poor that they eat nothing else. They sorted households by the share of their calories that came from rice before the experiment began.

Here is what they found in Hunan. Across all households the elasticity was positive, nought point two two, but not significant: the interval runs well below zero. Among households getting less than eighty percent of their calories from rice, it was nought point four five, and clearly positive. Among the very poorest, who ate almost nothing but rice, it was minus nought point six one: they had nothing to give up, and simply ate less when rice cost more. Between sixty and eighty percent, nought point six four. The mechanism showed too: households that ate meat cut it sharply when rice got dearer. A smoothed curve across calorie shares rose and fell, an inverted U, positive for nearly two thirds of the sample. In Gansu the evidence was weaker, and the authors said why: families there ate almost no meat to give up, and wheat came in many forms that could substitute for one another. One honest caution, which they raised themselves: searching across many cut-offs for a positive number is a forking path, Part four's warning. What protects them is that the theory picked the place to look before the data did.

Could the method have found nothing if nothing was there, or found the truth if it was? On the Island we can check, because we plant the truth. Thirteen hundred of the Island's poorest households, in eleven villages, live on coconuts and fish and a little oil and greens. They get Jensen and Miller's vouchers, at random, and the same three surveys, with consumption reported with error. We planted the subsistence model: households in its middle zone have an elasticity of plus nought point four three; those on either side, negative ones. Run their regression on everyone and you get almost exactly zero: the Giffen households and the others cancel. Restrict to households getting sixty to eighty percent of their calories from coconuts, and it's plus nought point three four, short of the planted value because mismeasured shares put some households in the wrong group. Their fish fall sharply, as the mechanism says. And the kernel-weighted curve, drawn the way they drew theirs, traces the planted inverted U. The lesson goes beyond Giffen goods: an average effect can be zero while a large group responds strongly, in the opposite direction from everyone else.
Engel: The curves that show how purchases change with income are named after a statistician. In 1857 Ernst Engel, who ran the statistical bureau of the Kingdom of Saxony, studied the budgets of Belgian working families and found a regularity. The poorer a family, he wrote, the greater the proportion of its spending that must go on food. And he went further: the share spent on food, other things equal, is the best measure of a population's material standard of living. A hundred years later, Hendrik Houthakker compared about forty household surveys from thirty countries and wrote that Engel's law is confirmed by all of them.

Here is Engel's law in America over almost a century. Across, real spending per person; up, the share of it spent on food bought to eat at home. As Americans got richer, the share fell, from about a fifth in 1929 to seven and a half percent in 2025. Real spending per head rose about six and a half times. Americans did buy more food, about two and a half times as much, but far less than in proportion. And food's price relative to everything else ended the century almost where it began, so the change is mostly an income effect: food's income elasticity across the century comes out at about nought point four seven. Below one: food is a necessity. Part of the fall, to be fair, is food that moved from home kitchens to restaurants.

The same law holds across households at one moment. In 2024 the poorest fifth of American households spent a third of their income on food; the middle fifth, twelve percent; the richest fifth, six percent. The richest households spent about three times as much on food as the poorest, with about sixteen times the income. Read as an elasticity, that's about a third between the poorest and the middle, and a half between the middle and the richest, where money goes on restaurants and dearer food rather than more calories. An Engel curve is a demand curve for income instead of price, and its slope sorts goods into necessities, luxuries, and the inferior goods of chapter four.

Engel's second sentence, that the food share measures the standard of living, became a tool for checking price indices in 2001. Bruce Hamilton's idea: if the official price index rises faster than the true cost of living, then real incomes deflated by it understate how rich people really are, more so every year. A household in a later year with the same measured real income is truly richer, so by Engel's law it spends a smaller share on food. So the Engel curve, drawn against measured income, drifts down from one survey to the next, and the drift divided by the curve's slope is the error in the index. On the Island we planted an index that overstates the cost of living by one percent a year, and drew six surveys four years apart. The method recovers the error survey by survey, and 0.97 percent a year in all. On American data, Hamilton found the CPI overstating by about two point seven percent a year from 1974 to 1982 and nought point six from 1982 to 1991; Dora Costa, with the same idea, carried the estimates back to 1888. Ingvild Almås turned it on countries in 2012 and found that the price comparisons behind international incomes make poor countries look richer than they are.

Here are their estimates side by side. Almost no bias before 1919, some in the 1920s and 30s, little in the 1960s, then a large overstatement in the inflation of the 1970s, in both studies the same two point seven points a year, and much less after. The Boskin Commission's 1996 range, from a completely different method, was nought point eight to one point six.

Called it? In 1857 Engel said that poorer families spend a larger share on food, and that the share measures a population's standard of living. A century and a half later, both halves hold: across American households in 2024, and across a century of American growth. It may be the oldest regularity in empirical economics, and it's still true.
